catalog_quote: 4.2.6 Tones / Bantu is reconstructed as having two tones, without any complications such as glides and downstep (Guthrie 1967–71; Marlo & Odden 2019). While this is characteristic of numerous Bantu languages in the central area, many languages, especially in Zone A, have a more elaborate system, which resembles more closely the three and four-tone systems which are common in Bantoid. Table 8 compiles a sample of descriptions of tone systems for Bantoid and Bantu, only listing languages with three tones or more. / Table 8. new_statements.rule_in_words: Buru is reported as a tone language with three level tones (High, Mid, Low). No source says anything about word stress; the tone inventory itself is Blench's reading of Robert Koops's unpublished 1970s wordlist, not a phonological description.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Blench 2016 slides: 'Not much more to say without more data.'
new_statements.domain_note: Citation-form wordlist data only (~400 words); no phrase-level or grammatical description exists (Blench 2024 gives 'no data' for word order).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 5.3 'Buru-Angwe' merges Buru (buru1326, the village east of Baissa) with Angwe (angw1241, Batu Angwe village), which Blench's Atlas (eds. 3 and 4) and Piron still list under the Batu [btu] cluster; Blench 2016 (Tivoid p. 14) moves Angwe to Buru. All data examined concern Buru proper (Koops wordlist); nothing examined describes Angwe separately.

sources.note: Nothing on stress. Table 8 'Tone systems in Bantoid and Bantu' (printed p. 24, p. 25) has the row 'Buru | Buru | H, M, L | Koops (ms.)', i.e. three level tones reported second-hand from Koops's unpublished wordlist; other Buru rows: four noun-class prefix pairs, 7 vowels, ATR 'No analysis', word order 'no data'.
